title: Quentin and the Letter
premise: On the eve of the Velloran Revolution, Orsen Fairweather works in his father's print shop, where the family survives by printing exactly what the regime permits and nothing more. When a terrified child named Quentin is left at their door with a letter ordering them to forget his face, Orsen discovers the boy is the son of a purged minister—and that his own father helped draft the death lists to buy the shop's safety. As the city ignites and escape berths on a coal barge dwindle to one, Orsen must decide whether to save his father, his sister, or the child who knows too much, ultimately forging a false letter in his father's own typeface that sends his family into hiding and himself and Quentin downriver toward an uncertain freedom.
about_author: Jonah Eriksen is the pen name of a former letterpress compositor who spent a decade restoring nineteenth-century print shops across northern Europe before turning to fiction. He writes historical novels about the quiet people history forgets—the hands that set the type, not the names on the page.

chapters.title: The Weight of Silence
chapters.summary: Orsen Fairweather, POV. In the print shop on the eve of the Velloran uprising, Orsen sorts type by candlelight, cataloguing the silences that keep his family safe: the pamphlets they refuse, the neighbors they no longer greet. Emotional beat: the suffocating comfort of invisibility, and the first hairline crack in it.

chapters.title: A Knock After Curfew
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A wet knock at the shop door past curfew reveals a mud-streaked boy of seven clutching a sealed letter. The instructions are brutal in their brevity: feed him, forget his face. Orsen's father recognizes the boy instantly—and goes white. Beat: dread arriving before understanding.

chapters.title: What Father Knew
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen confronts his father, Aldous, who admits the boy is Quentin, son of the purged Minister Corvel—and that Aldous's own hand helped set the lists that doomed him, the price of the shop's license. Beat: the collapse of the man Orsen trusted to know which silences mattered.

chapters.title: Sister of the Small Hours
chapters.summary: Maren Fairweather's POV. Orsen's sister, a nurse at the charity ward, returns at dawn and takes one look at Quentin and starts forging a fever chart to explain a strange child in the house. Beat: fierce, unsentimental loyalty—and her warning that the ward is already full of people asking questions.

chapters.title: The Letter's Second Life
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen studies the letter left with Quentin and recognizes the typeface: it was cut in their own shop, by his father's graver. Whoever wrote it wanted a trail that led home—or a trail that could be erased. Beat: paranoia blooming; the shop itself becomes evidence.

chapters.title: Ink on the Censor's Table
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A routine inspection brings Inspector Vasse into the shop, lingering over the type cases, asking after a child reported on the east road. Aldous performs calm; Orsen nearly breaks. Beat: the price of survival made physical—a man's hands shaking as he hands over state-approved proofs.

chapters.title: Quentin Speaks
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV, rendered in a child's fractured voice. The boy finally talks: his father hid him in a press crate, told him to count the letters on the walls until someone came. Beat: heartbreaking innocence—Quentin thinks the print shop is a game his father arranged.

chapters.title: The Barge at Salt Quay
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren learns the coal barge leaving on quarter-day has three berths for those who can pay in type—printed safe-conducts, forged. The family has coin for two. Beat: hope with a price tag, and the unspoken arithmetic beginning between siblings.

chapters.title: Barricades of Borrowed Paper
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The revolution ignites; students seize the print shops to print their own truth. Neighbors who once ignored the Fairweathers now demand pamphlets. Beat: the seduction and danger of finally choosing a side in public.

chapters.title: Aldous's Bargain
chapters.summary: Aldous's POV. Aldous secretly offers Inspector Vasse Quentin's whereabouts in exchange for the family's immunity, then burns the draft. Beat: a father's monstrous love—the man who set death lists now selling a child to save his own.

chapters.title: What Maren Saw
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren catches Aldous returning from the inspectorate at dawn and, without a word, moves Quentin's sleeping pallet to her own room. Beat: silent knowledge, and the siblings' alliance forming against their father without either naming it.

chapters.title: The Type Case Confession
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Sorting his father's graver tools, Orsen finds a hidden matrix—a master mold for the death-list type, kept as blackmail insurance. Beat: Orsen realizes his father's survival has always rested on owning the proof of his own guilt.

chapters.title: Fire in the Paper District
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. From the garret window, Quentin watches rebels burn the state print works and mistakes the flames for the game his father promised. Beat: terror refracted through childhood; the city's violence arriving at the child's eye level.

chapters.title: Two Berths, Three Names
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Quarter-day approaches; Vasse tightens the net, demanding Quentin within two days. The barge leaves in three. Orsen, Maren, and Aldous circle the arithmetic no one will say aloud. Beat: the family's love curdling into triage.

chapters.title: The Graver's Choice
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Alone at night, Orsen cuts a new letter—a forged safe-conduct in his father's exact hand, good for three berths. It is forgery, treason, and the first fully his own act. Beat: the typeface cutter's daughter's son choosing creation over silence.

chapters.title: Aldous Learns the Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Aldous's POV. Aldous discovers the forged document and, instead of rage, understands: his children have chosen Quentin, and one of them will stay behind. He quietly re-cuts the mold to add a fourth berth he cannot fill. Beat: a father's penance in lead and antimony.

chapters.title: Vasse at the Door
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Vasse arrives with soldiers, certain of the trail. Aldous confesses to forging the death lists—claiming Quentin's presence as his own blackmail scheme gone wrong—and is taken in Quentin's place. Beat: the father's final trade, and Orsen's horror at being saved by it.

chapters.title: The Last Proof
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. In the hours before the barge, Maren and Orsen print one true thing: a single-sheet account of the lists, Aldous's name included, and paste it across the quarter. Beat: loyalty to family finally yielding to truth—letting the record stand even against their own blood.

chapters.title: Salt Quay, Quarter-Day
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. At the quay, soldiers check papers; the forged safe-conduct holds by a hair. Vasse appears, looks at Orsen, looks at Quentin—and waves them through, having taken Aldous's confession as payment enough. Beat: mercy from the least merciful man, unexplained.

chapters.title: Downriver
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. On the coal barge, Quentin counts the letters on the riverbanks as his father taught him, holding Orsen's hand. Beat: grief and safety coexisting; the child beginning to understand what was spent for him.

chapters.title: The Shop Without Its Cutter
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, months later. In exile, Orsen receives word: Aldous was tried and imprisoned, not hanged—his testimony against the regime counted in his favor, the pasted sheet read into the record. Beat: the price of survival paid in full, and partially redeemed by truth.

chapters.title: Quentin and the Letter
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Quentin, older, asks to see the letter that started everything; Orsen finally lets him read it, then shows him the type case and teaches him to cut his first letter. Beat: the face they were ordered to forget, deliberately remembered—memory as inheritance, and love as the thing that outlasts duty.
